items.stem: Explain why reducing unemployment benefits might reduce the natural rate of unemployment.
items.answer: Lower benefits increase the incentive to search for and accept jobs, reducing the duration of frictional unemployment and voluntary unemployment.

items.stem: Explain why lower corporate tax rates may increase long-term growth.
items.answer: Higher post-tax profits increase the return on investment and retained earnings, and may attract FDI, raising the capital stock and productivity.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Thatcher-era reforms in the UK shows market-based supply-side policies.
items.answer: In the 1980s the UK cut the top income tax rate from 83% to 40%, privatised firms such as British Telecom (1984) and British Gas (1986) and reduced trade union power. The reforms aimed to increase incentives and competition, raising productivity, though inequality rose sharply
items.markingKey: Context (In the 1980s the UK cut the top income tax rate from 83% to 40%, privatised firms such as British Telecom (1984) and British Gas (1986) and reduced trade union power.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how market-based supply-side policies affect long-run aggregate supply.
items.answer: LRAS shifts right from LRAS1 to LRAS2 (or the vertical section of the Keynesian AS shifts right); potential output rises; with constant AD, the price level falls (or inflation is lower) and real GDP rises.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: LRAS shifts right from LRAS1 to LRAS2 (or the vertical section of the Keynesian AS shifts right); potential output rises; with constant AD, the price level falls (or inflation is lower) and real GDP rises. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that market-based supply-side policies are the best way to achieve long-term economic growth.
items.answer: Market-based reforms can raise efficiency, but they work best combined with interventionist investment in skills and infrastructure, and with measures to protect equity.

items.stem: A government must choose between cutting the top rate of income tax and spending the same amount on vocational training. Compare the likely effects of each on LRAS, the time lag and equity.
items.answer: Tax cut: quicker incentive effects, uncertain impact on work effort, benefits high earners (less equitable). Training: longer lag, raises human capital and LRAS, reduces structural unemployment, more equitable.

items.stem: Outline one way in which labour market flexibility in the UK shows trade-offs in market-based supply-side policies.
items.answer: The UK has among the least regulated labour markets in Europe, with zero-hours contracts for around a million workers. Flexibility helped keep unemployment low but created insecure jobs and weak productivity growth

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the benefits of supply-side policies outweigh their costs.
items.answer: Usually yes in the long run, but the costs depend on design: a mix of interventionist and market-based measures with attention to equity is most effective.

items.stem: Using India's 1991 liberalisation as an example, explain competition policy and deregulation.
items.answer: In 1991 India abolished most industrial licensing ("licence Raj"), cut tariffs and opened to FDI. Reducing barriers to entry and trade increased competition and investment, contributing to faster growth
items.markingKey: Context (In 1991 India abolished most industrial licensing ("licence Raj"), cut tariffs and opened to FDI.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Reducing barriers to entry and trade increased competition and investment, contributing to faster growth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to competition policy and deregulation.

items.stem: Using South Korea's investment in education as an example, explain interventionist supply-side policies.
items.answer: South Korea raised tertiary enrolment to among the highest in the OECD (around 70% of young adults) and spends about 5% of GDP on R&D. Investment in human capital and R&D supported its shift to high-technology industries
items.markingKey: Context (South Korea raised tertiary enrolment to among the highest in the OECD (around 70% of young adults) and spends about 5% of GDP on R&D.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Investment in human capital and R&D supported its shift to high-technology industries – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interventionist supply-side policies.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Supply-side policies always reduce inflation immediately." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They shift LRAS only after long time lags, and many (infrastructure spending, tax cuts) raise AD first, which can increase inflation in the short run.
items.markingKey: They shift LRAS only after long time lags, and many (infrastructure spending, tax cuts) raise AD first, which can increase inflation in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that supply-side policies only affect aggregate supply. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Many also affect AD: tax cuts raise consumption and investment, and government spending on infrastructure adds to AD in the short run.
items.markingKey: Many also affect AD: tax cuts raise consumption and investment, and government spending on infrastructure adds to AD in the short run. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe China's high-speed rail network and explain what it reveals about infrastructure as a supply-side policy.
items.answer: China built over 45,000 km of high-speed rail between 2008 and 2024, the world's largest network. Faster transport reduced travel time and connected labour markets, though some lines have low usage and high debts
items.markingKey: Context (China built over 45,000 km of high-speed rail between 2008 and 2024, the world's largest network.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Faster transport reduced travel time and connected labour markets, though some lines have low usage and high debts – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to infrastructure as a supply-side policy.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Japan's "third arrow" under Abenomics shows evaluating supply-side policies.
items.answer: After 2013, Japan's structural reforms (the "third arrow") aimed to raise female labour participation and deregulate sectors; female participation rose sharply but productivity growth stayed weak. Some reforms raised the quantity of labour but the impact on productivity was limited and slow
items.markingKey: Context (After 2013, Japan's structural reforms (the "third arrow") aimed to raise female labour participation and deregulate sectors; female participation rose sharply but productivity growth stayed weak.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Some reforms raised the quantity of labour but the impact on productivity was limited and slow – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to evaluating supply-side policies.

items.stem: Using Thatcher-era reforms in the UK as an example, explain market-based supply-side policies.
items.answer: In the 1980s the UK cut the top income tax rate from 83% to 40%, privatised firms such as British Telecom (1984) and British Gas (1986) and reduced trade union power. The reforms aimed to increase incentives and competition, raising productivity, though inequality rose sharply
items.markingKey: Context (In the 1980s the UK cut the top income tax rate from 83% to 40%, privatised firms such as British Telecom (1984) and British Gas (1986) and reduced trade union power.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The reforms aimed to increase incentives and competition, raising productivity, though inequality rose sharply – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to market-based supply-side policies.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Government investment in education is the most effective supply-side policy."
items.answer: Education is one of the most effective long-run policies, but it should be combined with infrastructure and labour market policies to deliver results.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: raises productivity and potential output; reduces inequality of opportunity; positive externalities. Arguments against: very long time lags; expensive; brain drain; quality matters more than quantity. Supported judgement: Education is one of the most effective long-run policies, but it should be combined with infrastructure and labour market policies to deliver results.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the benefits of supply-side policies outweigh their costs?
items.answer: Usually yes in the long run, but the costs depend on design: a mix of interventionist and market-based measures with attention to equity is most effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: increase LRAS and growth without inflation; reduce natural rate of unemployment; improve international competitiveness. Arguments against: long time lags; high fiscal cost for interventionist policies; equity concerns for market-based policies; environmental costs of growth. Supported judgement: Usually yes in the long run, but the costs depend on design: a mix of interventionist and market-based measures with attention to equity is most effective. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: You are a policy adviser to the ministry of finance. A minister argues that market-based supply-side policies are the best way to achieve long-term economic growth. Using your knowledge of economics, write a policy recommendation that evaluates this view and recommends a course of action.
items.answer: Market-based reforms can raise efficiency, but they work best combined with interventionist investment in skills and infrastructure, and with measures to protect equity.
items.markingKey: Supporting points: increase incentives and efficiency; no direct cost to the budget (deregulation); can lower the natural rate of unemployment. Counter-points: may increase inequality and job insecurity; tax cuts may not raise work effort and reduce revenue; privatised monopolies may need regulation; long time lags. Recommendation: Market-based reforms can raise efficiency, but they work best combined with interventionist investment in skills and infrastructure, and with measures to protect equity. Policy recommendation markbands [10]: Level 4 (9-10) a clear recommendation that is justified with economic theory, the information provided and its likely consequences for stakeholders; trade-offs and risks weighed. Level 3 (6-8) recommendation supported but justification partly developed. Level 2 (3-5) limited justification. Level 1 (1-2) recommendation asserted.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "market-based supply-side policies".
items.answer: Policies that reduce government intervention to make markets work more freely and efficiently, such as labour market reforms, deregulation and lower taxes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: policies that reduce government intervention to make markets work more freely and efficiently, such as labour market reforms, deregulation and lower taxes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "research and development (R&D)".
items.answer: Investment in creating new knowledge, products and processes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: investment in creating new knowledge, products and processes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The level of real GDP achievable when resources are fully employed, shown by the position of LRAS"?
items.answer: potential output
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of potential output.

items.stem: Explain the difference between interventionist supply-side policies and market-based supply-side policies.
items.answer: Market-based policies reduce government intervention (deregulation, tax cuts, labour market reform); interventionist policies involve active government spending and direction (education, infrastructure, R&D, industrial policy).
items.markingKey: Market-based policies reduce government intervention (deregulation, tax cuts, labour market reform); interventionist policies involve active government spending and direction (education, infrastructure, R&D, industrial policy). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between infrastructure investment and education and training.
items.answer: Education and training improve the quality of labour (human capital); infrastructure improves physical capital that lowers costs and connects markets.
items.markingKey: Education and training improve the quality of labour (human capital); infrastructure improves physical capital that lowers costs and connects markets. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why supply-side policies may not reduce cyclical unemployment.
items.answer: Cyclical unemployment is caused by insufficient AD; raising productive capacity does not create demand for the extra output, so firms will not hire more workers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cyclical unemployment is caused by insufficient AD; raising productive capacity does not create demand for the extra output, so firms will not hire more workers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why supply-side policies may take a long time to affect the economy.
items.answer: Increasing human capital, building infrastructure or developing new technology takes years before productive capacity rises.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Increasing human capital, building infrastructure or developing new technology takes years before productive capacity rises. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Germany's Hartz reforms and explain what it reveals about labour market reforms.
items.answer: The Hartz reforms of 2003-2005 merged benefits, reduced long-term unemployment benefits and reformed job centres; unemployment fell from about 11% in 2005 to under 6% by 2015. Stronger work incentives and better job matching reduced long-term unemployment, though low-paid "mini-jobs" increased
items.markingKey: Context (The Hartz reforms of 2003-2005 merged benefits, reduced long-term unemployment benefits and reformed job centres; unemployment fell from about 11% in 2005 to under 6% by 2015.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Stronger work incentives and better job matching reduced long-term unemployment, though low-paid "mini-jobs" increased – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to labour market reforms.

items.stem: Using the US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) as an example, explain industrial policy.
items.answer: The IRA offers tax credits worth hundreds of billions of dollars for clean energy, electric vehicles and batteries. Subsidies aim to expand domestic green industries, but critics argue they distort trade and may waste resources
items.markingKey: Context (The IRA offers tax credits worth hundreds of billions of dollars for clean energy, electric vehicles and batteries.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Subsidies aim to expand domestic green industries, but critics argue they distort trade and may waste resources – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to industrial policy.

items.stem: Using labour market flexibility in the UK as an example, explain trade-offs in market-based supply-side policies.
items.answer: The UK has among the least regulated labour markets in Europe, with zero-hours contracts for around a million workers. Flexibility helped keep unemployment low but created insecure jobs and weak productivity growth
items.markingKey: Context (The UK has among the least regulated labour markets in Europe, with zero-hours contracts for around a million workers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Flexibility helped keep unemployment low but created insecure jobs and weak productivity growth – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to trade-offs in market-based supply-side policies.

items.stem: A student claims that cutting income tax always increases the amount people work. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: There is a substitution effect (work pays more) but also an income effect (people can afford more leisure), so the net effect on hours is uncertain.
items.markingKey: There is a substitution effect (work pays more) but also an income effect (people can afford more leisure), so the net effect on hours is uncertain. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.
